items.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997
items.q: If Woody Herman had gone through his number like he did when he was dying... anywhere else in the world he’s a hero, he would have been a national hero.

ctx.x: I play in Toronto a lot you know, I have a group up there, and all college kids come to hear us now, and they’re really into it. The more we get into the music, the more they like it. I mean it’s really intriguing — improvisation is intriguing in every aspect of the word in every business. So when something happens like that man, it’s great, you know, the spontaneity of it and a quick, good idea, no matter what you’re doing, no matter what end of the business or spectrum.

And it’s funny, the whole world looks at jazz players and jazz music as a vital art form, as a very important art form of the last fifty or hundred years — not here. Now they’re just starting, sort of like coming around to it but not here. If Woody Herman had gone through his number like he did when he was dying and when the IRS was ready to wheel his bed out in the street and take his house from him, anywhere else in the world he’s a hero, he would have been a national hero. But not here. It’s rather sad.
I think that somebody bailed him out. I hate to mention his name because I can’t stand him.
